variants.explanation: A fully specified route names both the exit interface and the next hop: GigabitEthernet0/1 192.168.1.2. A next hop alone is recursive, an interface alone relies on proxy ARP on Ethernet, and Null0 discards traffic.

stem: R1 has two ISPs. Based on the exhibit, which default route is in the routing table while both links are up?
exhibit:
R1#show running-config | include ip route
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.1
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.51.100.1 5
choices: Both, load-balanced
Neither, because they conflict
explanation: The first route has AD 1 and the second AD 5, so 203.0.113.1 wins. The second is a floating backup that appears if the first is withdrawn.

variants.stem: R1 has two ISPs. Based on the exhibit, which default route is in the routing table after the link to 203.0.113.1 goes down?
variants.explanation: The route via 203.0.113.1 has AD 1 and the one via 198.51.100.1 has AD 5, so normally only the first is installed. When its path goes down it's withdrawn and the floating route via 198.51.100.1 takes over.

stem: Write a backup default route via 198.51.100.1 with administrative distance 5.
explanation: The AD goes after the next hop. A value above the primary route's AD (1 for static) makes it float.

variants.stem: Write a backup default route via 203.0.113.9 with administrative distance 10.
variants.explanation: The administrative distance goes at the end of the command: ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.9 10. With AD 10 it floats behind a primary default route with AD 1.

stem: IPv6 static routes are configured on R1, but it doesn't forward any IPv6 traffic. What is missing?
choices: ipv6 enable on every interface
ipv6 unicast-routing
ip routing
ipv6 cef
explanation: IOS routes IPv4 by default but IPv6 only after 'ipv6 unicast-routing'. Without it, the router acts as an IPv6 host.

variants.stem: R1 has IPv6 addresses on its interfaces but no 'ipv6 unicast-routing'. How does it handle IPv6?
choices: It forwards IPv6 using only its static routes
It acts as an IPv6 host and forwards nothing
It ignores IPv6 packets, even those sent to its own addresses
It forwards IPv6 packets by converting them to IPv4
variants.explanation: Without 'ipv6 unicast-routing' the router behaves as an IPv6 host: it can use its own addresses but won't route between interfaces, so IPv6 static routes do nothing until the command is entered.

stem: Which command shows only the IPv6 static routes?
choices: show ipv6 interface brief
show ip route static
show ipv6 static
show ipv6 route static
explanation: Like IPv4, 'show ipv6 route' takes a source filter such as static, connected or ospf.

variants.stem: Which command shows only the IPv4 static routes?
variants.explanation: 'show ip route static' filters the IPv4 table to S routes. The IPv6 equivalent is 'show ipv6 route static', and 'show ipv6 static' isn't a command.

stem: R1 has two static routes to 10.30.0.0/16 with the same AD, via two different next hops. What does R1 do?
choices: Uses the one entered first
Installs both and shares traffic between them
Uses neither
Uses the one with the lower next-hop address
explanation: Equal AD and equal metric (0 for static) means both are installed and traffic is load-balanced, just like equal-cost dynamic routes.

variants.stem: R1 has two static routes to 10.30.0.0/16 via two different next hops, one with the default AD and one with AD 10. What does R1 do?
choices: Installs only the route with the default AD of 1
Installs both and shares traffic between them
Uses neither
Uses the one with the lower next-hop address
variants.explanation: The routes are for the same prefix, so the lower AD wins: 1 beats 10. The AD 10 route is a floating static route that appears only if the first is withdrawn. Traffic is shared only when the ADs and metrics are equal.

stem: What is the main drawback of using only static routes in a large network?
choices: They don't adapt to failures and must be maintained by hand
They use a lot of bandwidth sending periodic updates
They have a high AD
They can't be used for default routes in large networks
explanation: Static routes send no updates and need no CPU, but every topology change means manual edits, and a failure isn't routed around unless you planned a backup.

variants.stem: What is the main advantage of static routes over a routing protocol?
choices: They adapt to failures automatically
They send no updates and use no CPU to calculate routes
They're the only way to make a default route
They scale well to large networks that change often
variants.explanation: Static routes cost nothing to run: no updates on the links and no route calculation. The price is that they don't adapt to failures and every change is a manual edit.

stem: Which two are good uses for static routes? (Choose two.)
choices: A floating backup for a dynamically learned route
A full mesh of 50 routers
A default route from a stub branch to its only ISP
A large network that changes often
explanation: Stub networks with one way out and backup paths are classic static use cases. Large or changing networks need a routing protocol.

variants.stem: Which two are poor uses for static routes? (Choose two.)
variants.explanation: A 50-router full mesh or a large, changing network would need endless manual edits and wouldn't adapt to failures, so a routing protocol fits better. A stub branch's default route and a floating backup are classic static routes.

stem: A user reports that 10.9.9.9 is unreachable. Based on the exhibit from R1, what is wrong?
choices: A routing loop: R2's route for 10.9.9.9 points back to R1
The destination host is down and not answering
An ACL on R2 is blocking ICMP to 10.9.9.9
The TTL is set too low on the packets from the user's PC
explanation: The packet bounces between 10.0.0.2 (R2) and 10.0.0.1 (R1) until the TTL runs out. Each router's route points at the other, a common mistake with static routes.

variants.stem: R1 traces the path to 10.9.9.9. Based on the exhibit, which statement is true?
choices: A routing loop: R2's route for 10.9.9.9 points back to R1
The path works: 10.9.9.9 answered at hop 3
An ACL on R2 is blocking ICMP to 10.9.9.9
The TTL is set too low on R1's packets
variants.explanation: Each hop is a new address and the last line is the destination itself, so the path works and is three hops long. A loop would show the same two addresses repeating until the TTL ran out.

stem: When is a static route with only an exit interface (no next hop) a reasonable choice?
choices: On a point-to-point link such as a serial link
On any Ethernet LAN with a single router on it
Whenever the next-hop address isn't known yet
Never
explanation: On point-to-point links there's only one device at the other end, so no ARP for each destination is needed. On Ethernet, include the next hop.

variants.stem: When should you avoid a static route that names only an exit interface?
choices: On a point-to-point link such as a serial link
On an Ethernet link, where R1 would ARP for every destination
On a link where only one device sits at the other end
Never: exit-interface-only routes are always fine
variants.explanation: On Ethernet an exit-interface-only route makes R1 ARP for every destination and depend on proxy ARP from the next router. On a point-to-point link there's only one device at the far end, so it's fine.

stem: Write a fully specified IPv6 static route to 2001:db8:7::/64 out Gi0/1 via next hop fe80::7.
explanation: The interface comes before the link-local next hop. A link-local next hop always needs the interface.

variants.stem: Write a fully specified IPv6 static route to 2001:db8:8::/64 out Gi0/0 via next hop fe80::1.
variants.explanation: A link-local next hop is only unique on one link, so the route names the interface and then the next hop: ipv6 route 2001:db8:8::/64 g0/0 fe80::1.

stem: In 'S 10.20.0.0/16 [1/0] via 10.0.0.2', what do the numbers in [1/0] mean?
choices: Hop count 1 and cost 0
AD 1 and metric 0
Priority 1 and weight 0
1 path and 0 backups
explanation: Static routes have AD 1 by default and a metric of 0.

variants.stem: In 'S 10.20.0.0/16 [5/0] via 10.0.0.2', what does the 5 tell you?
choices: The route's hop count is 5
The route was configured with administrative distance 5
The route has 5 equal-cost paths
The route's priority is 5
variants.explanation: In [AD/metric] the first number is the administrative distance. A static route normally shows [1/0]; [5/0] means someone added AD 5 to the command, as for a floating route.

stem: What is OSPF area 0?
choices: Any area that contains only one router
The area reserved for loopback interfaces
An area that only carries default routes
The backbone area, which all other areas must connect to
explanation: Area 0 is the backbone. In single-area OSPF every interface is normally in area 0.

variants.stem: In single-area OSPF, which area is every interface normally in?
choices: A different area on every link
Area 1
Area 0, the backbone
Area 255
variants.explanation: Area 0 is the backbone, and in a single-area design every interface is normally placed in it. Neighbours must agree on the area, so one area per link would break adjacencies.

stem: What does every router in one OSPF area have in common?
choices: An identical link-state database for the area
The same router ID, set by the area's DR
The same routing table, since SPF gives one answer
The same interface costs
explanation: All routers in an area synchronise the same LSDB. Each then runs SPF from its own position, so their routing tables differ.

variants.stem: Routers in one OSPF area share the same link-state database. What still differs between them?
choices: Their copies of the link-state database
Nothing: SPF gives every router the same routes
Their routing tables, since each runs SPF from its own position
The area ID on their interfaces
variants.explanation: The LSDB is the same map for everyone, but each router runs SPF with itself at the root, so its best paths and next hops are its own and the routing tables differ.

stem: Which LSA type does every OSPF router originate to describe its own links in the area?
choices: Type 5 (external LSA)
Type 2 (network LSA)
Type 3 (summary LSA)
Type 1 (router LSA)
explanation: Every router floods a type 1 LSA listing its links and costs. Type 2 comes from the DR for a multi-access segment; types 3 and 5 come from ABRs and ASBRs.

variants.stem: Which LSA type does the DR originate to describe a multi-access segment?
variants.explanation: The DR alone originates the type 2 (network) LSA for its segment. Every router originates its own type 1 (router) LSA, and types 3 and 5 come from ABRs and ASBRs.

stem: Which router originates the type 2 (network) LSA for an Ethernet segment?
choices: Every router on the segment
The DR
The BDR
The router with the lowest router ID
explanation: The DR represents the multi-access segment in the LSDB with a type 2 LSA listing the routers attached to it.

variants.stem: Which router originates a type 1 (router) LSA on an Ethernet segment?
variants.explanation: Every OSPF router writes a type 1 LSA describing its own links and costs. Only the type 2 (network) LSA is limited to the DR.

stem: Based on the exhibit from R1, which statement is true?
exhibit:
R1#show ip ospf interface g0/0
GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
  Internet Address 10.0.0.1/24, Area 0
  Process ID 1, Router ID 1.1.1.1, Network Type BROADCAST, Cost: 1
  Transmit Delay is 1 sec, State BDR, Priority 1
  Designated Router (ID) 3.3.3.3, Interface address 10.0.0.3
  Backup Designated router (ID) 1.1.1.1, Interface address 10.0.0.1
  Timer intervals configured, Hello 10, Dead 40, Wait 40, Retransmit 5
choices: R1 is the DR on this segment
R1 has priority 0, so it's a DROther
The segment is point-to-point, with no DR
R1 is the BDR and 3.3.3.3 is the DR
explanation: 'State BDR' is R1's own role, and the DR line shows router ID 3.3.3.3. The network type is BROADCAST, which elects a DR and BDR.

variants.stem: Based on this exhibit from R1, which statement is true?
variants.exhibit:
R1#show ip ospf interface g0/0
GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
  Internet Address 10.0.0.1/24, Area 0
  Process ID 1, Router ID 1.1.1.1, Network Type BROADCAST, Cost: 1
  Transmit Delay is 1 sec, State DR, Priority 1
  Designated Router (ID) 1.1.1.1, Interface address 10.0.0.1
  Backup Designated router (ID) 3.3.3.3, Interface address 10.0.0.3
  Timer intervals configured, Hello 10, Dead 40, Wait 40, Retransmit 5
variants.explanation: 'State DR' and the Designated Router line showing R1's own ID (1.1.1.1) mean R1 is the DR; 3.3.3.3 is the BDR. Priority is 1 and the network type is broadcast, so an election did take place.

stem: R1 uses OSPF Hello 10 / Dead 40 on a link, and R2 uses Hello 5 / Dead 20. What happens?
choices: They become neighbours using the lower timers
R1 adopts R2's timers
They become neighbours but don't exchange LSAs
They don't become neighbours, because the timers must match
explanation: Hello and dead intervals are carried in Hellos and must match exactly. Fix them with 'ip ospf hello-interval' and 'ip ospf dead-interval'.

variants.stem: R1 and R2 both use OSPF Hello 10 / Dead 40 on a link in area 0, but R1 runs 'router ospf 1' and R2 runs 'router ospf 2'. What happens?
choices: They become neighbours, because process IDs are only local
R1 adopts R2's process ID
They become neighbours but don't exchange LSAs
They don't become neighbours, because the process IDs must match
variants.explanation: The process ID only identifies the process on that router and isn't carried in Hellos, so it doesn't have to match. The timers, area and subnet match, so the adjacency forms.

stem: R1's link to R2 is 10.0.12.1/30 and R2's side is 10.0.12.5/30. Both run OSPF in area 0. What happens?
choices: They become neighbours, because both are in area 0
They become neighbours but stay stuck in 2-Way
They don't become neighbours: different subnets
R2 changes its address
explanation: 10.0.12.1/30 is in 10.0.12.0-3 and 10.0.12.5/30 in 10.0.12.4-7. OSPF neighbours on a broadcast link must share a subnet and mask.

variants.stem: R1's link to R2 is 10.0.12.1/30 and R2's side is 10.0.12.2/30. Both run OSPF in area 0 with default timers. What happens?
choices: They become neighbours: same subnet and same area
They become neighbours but stay stuck in 2-Way
They don't become neighbours: different subnets
R2 changes its address
variants.explanation: 10.0.12.1 and 10.0.12.2 are both in 10.0.12.0/30, the area and timers match, so they become neighbours. Two routers alone on a link aren't both DROthers, so they don't stop at 2-Way.

stem: Two OSPF neighbours stay stuck in EXSTART/EXCHANGE. What is a common cause?
choices: Mismatched Hello timers
Duplicate network statements
Different process IDs
Mismatched interface MTU
explanation: Hellos (and so 2-Way) work, but database description packets are rejected when the MTUs differ. Timer or area mismatches stop them before 2-Way.

variants.stem: R1 and R2 never become OSPF neighbours. 'show ip ospf interface' shows Hello 10 on R1 and Hello 5 on R2. What is the cause?
variants.explanation: Hello and Dead timers must match, so the routers ignore each other's Hellos and no adjacency forms. A mismatched MTU is different: Hellos work, but the routers stick in ExStart/Exchange.

stem: On which OSPF network type is no DR or BDR elected?
choices: Broadcast
Non-broadcast multi-access
Point-to-point
Every type elects one
explanation: With only two routers on a link there's nothing to gain from a DR. Point-to-point links go straight to Full, and Ethernet links between two routers can be set to this type.

variants.stem: Which OSPF network type, the default on Ethernet, elects a DR and BDR?
variants.explanation: Ethernet interfaces default to the broadcast network type, which elects a DR and BDR to cut down flooding. Point-to-point skips the election.

stem: Which interface command stops a router from ever becoming DR or BDR on that segment? (full command)
explanation: Priority 0 makes the router ineligible. It still forms Full adjacencies with the DR and BDR.

variants.stem: Which interface command gives a router the highest possible OSPF priority on that segment? (full command)
variants.explanation: OSPF priority ranges from 0 to 255, so 'ip ospf priority 255' is the highest. It wins the next election, but because there's no preemption it won't take over a working DR.

stem: Which interface command makes an Ethernet link between two routers use the OSPF point-to-point network type? (full command)
explanation: This skips the DR/BDR election and the wait timer, so the adjacency comes up faster. Set it on both ends.

variants.stem: Which interface command sets the OSPF Hello interval to 5 seconds? (full command)
variants.explanation: 'ip ospf hello-interval 5' changes the Hello timer on the interface. It must match on both ends of the link, as must the Dead timer ('ip ospf dead-interval').

stem: Which command shows the OSPF process ID, router ID and the networks OSPF is routing for?
choices: show ip ospf neighbor
show ip protocols
show ip route
show running-config interface
explanation: 'show ip protocols' summarises each routing process: router ID, network statements, passive interfaces and routing information sources.

variants.stem: Which command shows the router's own DR/BDR state, priority, cost and network type on an interface?
choices: show ip ospf neighbor
show ip protocols
show ip route
show ip ospf interface
variants.explanation: show ip ospf interface describes OSPF on each interface: its state (DR, BDR or DROTHER), priority, cost, network type and the DR's router ID. show ip ospf neighbor shows the neighbours' roles instead.

stem: With the default reference bandwidth, path A to 10.9.9.0/24 crosses two 100 Mbps links and path B crosses one 10 Mbps link. Which does OSPF choose?
choices: Path B, with cost 1
Path A, with cost 2
Path B, because it has fewer hops
Both, as equal-cost paths
explanation: Cost = 100 Mbps / bandwidth: each 100 Mbps link costs 1, so path A is 2; a 10 Mbps link costs 10. Hop count doesn't matter to OSPF.

variants.stem: With the default reference bandwidth, path A to 10.9.9.0/24 crosses two 100 Mbps links and path B crosses one 1 Gbps link. Which does OSPF choose?
variants.explanation: With a 100 Mbps reference, 100 Mbps and 1 Gbps both cost 1. Path A costs 1 + 1 = 2 and path B costs 1, so path B wins. It's the total cost that matters, not hop count.

stem: Why change 'auto-cost reference-bandwidth' in a network with 1, 10 and 100 Gbps links?
choices: To reduce Hello traffic on the fastest links
To speed up convergence after a link fails
So the faster links get lower costs than the slower ones
To change OSPF's administrative distance
explanation: With the default 100 Mbps reference every link of 100 Mbps or faster costs 1, so OSPF can't tell them apart. Set the same reference on every router.

variants.stem: With the default reference bandwidth, what OSPF costs do 1, 10 and 100 Gbps links get?
choices: 100, 10 and 1, falling as speed rises
1 each, so OSPF can't tell them apart
10, 1 and 0, with 100 Gbps free
1, 10 and 100, rising as speed rises
variants.explanation: The default reference is 100 Mbps and the minimum cost is 1, so every link of 100 Mbps or faster costs 1. That's why the reference bandwidth needs raising in fast networks.

stem: Gi0/1 has 10.5.5.1/24. Which two configurations enable OSPF process 1 on it in area 0? (Choose two.)
choices: router ospf 1, then network 10.5.5.0 255.255.255.0
On interface Gi0/1: ip ospf 1 area 0
router ospf 1, then ospf enable area 0
router ospf 1, then network 10.5.5.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
explanation: A network statement needs a wildcard and an area; the interface command enables OSPF directly. There's no 'ospf enable' command.

variants.stem: Gi0/1 has 10.5.5.1/24. Which two network statements under router ospf 1 put it in area 0? (Choose two.)
choices: network 10.5.5.1 0.0.0.0 area 0
variants.explanation: 0.0.0.0 matches exactly 10.5.5.1, and 10.5.0.0 0.0.255.255 matches everything in 10.5.x.x, so both enable Gi0/1 in area 0. 10.5.6.0 0.0.0.255 misses the address, and the last statement uses area 1.

stem: Match each OSPF packet type to its job.

answer.Hello: Finds neighbours and keeps adjacencies alive

explanation: Hellos build adjacencies; DBD, LSR, LSU and LSAck then synchronise the database reliably.

variants.stem: Match each OSPF packet type number to its packet.
variants.explanation: The numbers follow the conversation: 1 Hello, 2 DBD (here's my table of contents), 3 LSR (can I have that?), 4 LSU (here it is), 5 LSAck (got it).

stem: What problem do first hop redundancy protocols solve?
choices: DHCP servers run out of addresses on busy subnets
Switches loop without spanning tree on redundant links
Routers can't share routes without a routing protocol
Hosts have one default gateway, which is a single point of failure
explanation: An FHRP lets two or more routers share a virtual IP and MAC, so the hosts' single gateway setting keeps working if one router fails.

variants.stem: What problem does GLBP solve that HSRP alone doesn't?
choices: DHCP servers run out of addresses on busy subnets
Only one router forwards in an HSRP group, so the others sit idle
Routers can't share routes without a routing protocol
Hosts have one default gateway, which is a single point of failure
variants.explanation: HSRP already solves the single gateway problem, but only its active router forwards. GLBP lets several routers forward for one virtual IP, so their capacity isn't wasted.

stem: Which interface command lets this router take over as HSRP active for group 1 whenever it has the higher priority? (full command)
explanation: Without preempt, a higher-priority router that comes up later stays standby until the active router fails.

variants.stem: Which interface command lowers this router's HSRP group 1 priority by 20 while Gi0/1 is down? (full command)
variants.explanation: 'standby 1 track g0/1 20' tracks the uplink and takes 20 off the priority when it fails, so a peer with preempt and a higher priority can take over.

stem: Which interface command sets HSRP group 1's virtual IP to 10.1.1.254? (full command)
explanation: Every router in the group uses the same group number and virtual IP; hosts use the virtual IP as their gateway.

variants.stem: Which interface command sets HSRP group 1's priority to 110? (full command)
variants.explanation: 'standby 1 priority 110' raises the priority above the default of 100. Add 'standby 1 preempt' if this router should take over from a working active router.

stem: What is the VRRP virtual MAC address for group 5?
explanation: VRRP uses 0000.5e00.01XX with the group in hex. 0000.0c07.acXX is HSRPv1, 0000.0c9f.fXXX HSRPv2 and 0007.b4XX.XXYY GLBP.

variants.stem: What is the HSRPv1 virtual MAC address for group 5?
variants.explanation: HSRPv1 uses 0000.0c07.acXX with the group in hex, so group 5 is 0000.0c07.ac05. 0000.0c9f.f005 is HSRPv2, 0000.5e00.0105 is VRRP and 0007.b4 is GLBP.

stem: In VRRP, can the virtual IP be the real interface address of one of the routers?
choices: No, it must be an unused address in the subnet
Yes: the address owner gets priority 255 and is master
Only in HSRP, where the active router owns the IP
Only for IPv6
explanation: VRRP allows the virtual IP to be a real address. The owner always becomes master. HSRP needs a separate virtual address.

variants.stem: In HSRP, can the virtual IP be the real interface address of one of the routers?
choices: No: HSRP needs a separate virtual address
Yes: the address owner gets priority 255 and is active
Yes, but only on the standby router
Only for IPv6
variants.explanation: HSRP's virtual IP must be its own address in the subnet. Using a real router's address, with the owner getting priority 255, is a VRRP feature.

stem: In GLBP, what does the active virtual gateway (AVG) do?
choices: Forwards all traffic itself while the others stand by
Acts as a backup only
Answers ARP for the virtual IP with different forwarders' MACs
Runs the routing protocol on behalf of the group
explanation: The AVG assigns virtual MACs to up to four active virtual forwarders (AVFs) and spreads hosts across them in its ARP replies.

variants.stem: In GLBP, what do the active virtual forwarders (AVFs) do?
choices: Answer ARP for the virtual IP on behalf of the group
Forward traffic sent to their own virtual MAC, sharing the load
Act as a backup only
Run the routing protocol on behalf of the group
variants.explanation: Each AVF owns one of the virtual MACs the AVG hands out and forwards the traffic sent to it, so up to four routers share the load. Answering ARP is the AVG's job.

stem: R2 has a lower priority than R1 (192.168.1.2, priority 100) but is active. Based on the exhibit from R2, why?
exhibit:
R2#show standby
GigabitEthernet0/0 - Group 10
  State is Active
  Virtual IP address is 192.168.1.254
  Active virtual MAC address is 0000.0c07.ac0a
  Hello time 3 sec, hold time 10 sec
  Preemption disabled
  Active router is local
  Standby router is 192.168.1.2, priority 100 (expires in 9.1 sec)
  Priority 90 (configured 90)
choices: R2 has the higher IP address, which beats priority
In HSRP a lower priority value wins the election
R1 has no preempt, so it doesn't take over from R2
R2 is using HSRPv2
explanation: Higher priority only wins at election time or with preempt. R2 came up first (or R1 restarted), and R1 waits as standby. The MAC 0000.0c07.ac0a shows HSRPv1, group 10.

variants.stem: R1 (192.168.1.2, priority 100) is the standby router. Based on this exhibit from R2, why is R2 active?
variants.exhibit:
R2#show standby
GigabitEthernet0/0 - Group 10
  State is Active
  Virtual IP address is 192.168.1.254
  Active virtual MAC address is 0000.0c07.ac0a
  Hello time 3 sec, hold time 10 sec
  Preemption enabled
  Active router is local
  Standby router is 192.168.1.2, priority 100 (expires in 9.1 sec)
  Priority 110 (configured 110)
choices: R2 has the higher IP address, which beats priority
In HSRP a lower priority value wins the election
R1 has no preempt, so it doesn't take over from R2
R2 has the higher priority, 110 against 100
variants.explanation: R2's priority is 110 and R1's is 100, and the highest priority wins. With preemption enabled R2 would also take over if it came up later. The IP address only breaks ties.

stem: Hosts ARP for the HSRP virtual IP. Which MAC address is in the reply?
choices: The active router's burned-in MAC
The group's virtual MAC
The standby router's MAC
ffff.ffff.ffff
explanation: The virtual MAC moves with the active role, so after a failover hosts keep using the same gateway MAC and don't need to ARP again.

variants.stem: After an HSRP failover, what happens to the gateway MAC address the hosts use?
choices: The new active router's burned-in MAC replaces it
It moves to the new active router, so hosts keep the same gateway MAC
Hosts flush their ARP caches and learn a new virtual MAC
It becomes ffff.ffff.ffff until the next Hello
variants.explanation: The virtual MAC belongs to the group and moves with the active role. Hosts keep the same gateway IP and MAC, so they don't need to ARP again and notice nothing.

stem: What is the range of HSRP priority values?
explanation: Priority is 0-255 with a default of 100. (0-4095 is the HSRPv2 group number range.)

variants.stem: What is the range of HSRPv2 group numbers?
variants.explanation: HSRPv2 supports groups 0-4095, which is why its MAC carries the group in three hex digits. HSRPv1 groups are 0-255, the same range as the priority.

stem: Which two statements about HSRP are true? (Choose two.)
choices: It is Cisco-proprietary
Every router in the group forwards traffic at the same time
It is an IETF standard
Only the active router in a group forwards traffic for the virtual IP
explanation: HSRP is Cisco's; VRRP is the standard. One active router per group forwards; load sharing needs several groups or GLBP.

variants.stem: Which two statements about VRRP are true? (Choose two.)
choices: It is Cisco-proprietary
It uses master and backup routers
It is an open standard
Its virtual IP must differ from every router's real address
variants.explanation: VRRP is the open standard (RFC 5798) and calls its roles master and backup. Its virtual IP may be a real router's address, whose owner then gets priority 255; HSRP and GLBP are the Cisco ones.
